title: Fieldwork Adventure: Analysis & Evaluation
welcome_lead: What does your data MEAN — and was your method fair? Welcome to analysis and evaluation.
meta_desc: GCSE Geography fieldwork analysis and evaluation — validity, reliability, conclusions.
final_note: You learned how to evaluate your method, spot errors, and write strong conclusions.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Validity: does your method measure what you THINK it does? Counting cars at 3 a.m. is not a VALID measure of urban congestion.

Reliability: if someone repeats your method, would they get similar results? Repeating measurements and averaging boosts reliability.

Human error: misreading a tape, mis-counting pedestrians.

Instrument error: a faulty flow meter.

Sampling error: too few sites, biased locations (only sampling on the main road).

Always identify anomalies: don't ignore — explain or investigate.

A strong conclusion directly answers the hypothesis, supported by quoted data.

A strong evaluation honestly states:

- limitations of method (small sample, weather affected results)
- improvements (more sites, repeat in different season)
- confidence in conclusion (e.g. moderate — needs more data).

mcqs.q: What is the difference between primary and secondary data in geography fieldwork?
options: Primary data is collected first-hand by the researcher (surveys, measurements, observations); secondary data already exists and is found in sources (census data, maps, published reports).
Primary data is collected in primary schools and secondary data in secondary schools.
Primary data is more important and secondary data is less reliable.
Qualitative data means high-quality data and quantitative means a lot of data.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between qualitative and quantitative data?
options: Stratified sampling means picking samples from different strata of rock.
Qualitative data means high-quality data and quantitative means a lot of data.
Quantitative data is always more scientific and reliable than qualitative.
Quantitative data is numerical and measurable (traffic counts, river width); qualitative data is descriptive and non-numerical (interview quotes, photo descriptions, field sketches).

mcqs.q: What is the difference between random, stratified and systematic sampling?
options: All three sampling methods produce the same results.
Primary data is collected in primary schools and secondary data in secondary schools.
Stratified sampling means picking samples from different strata of rock.

Random: every member has equal chance of selection. Systematic: pick every nth item. Stratified: divide the population into groups and sample proportionally from each — ensures subgroup representation.
